strengths: Clear motivation for combining control functionals with MLMC, well-articulated compared to existing multilevel approaches
Theoretical variance analysis (Theorem 2) providing convergence rate improvement when smoothness assumptions hold
Practical applicability: works with unnormalized densities and requires no domain expert knowledge
Technically sound mathematical development with correct proofs
Demonstrated empirical improvements on two test problems
weaknesses: Limited novelty: straightforward combination of existing techniques (MLMC + control functionals) without fundamental algorithmic innovation
Restrictive theoretical assumptions (A1-A8) including boundary conditions and RKHS membership that may not hold in practice; experiments acknowledge assumptions are violated
Curse of dimensionality persists: convergence rate O(n^{-(τ/d)-1/2}) degrades as dimension increases; experiments only test d≤8

Weak experimental validation: only two examples (both low-dimensional), no actual comparison with related multilevel control variate methods despite claiming broad applicability, large error bars with overlap, single real application

Incomplete work: conclusion states 'in full version we will consider optimal sample size at each level,' suggesting submission is preliminary; critical practical questions unanswered (kernel selection, level selection, sample allocation strategies)
Inconsistency between theory and experiments: theoretical predictions on smoothness and convergence rates not empirically validated; experimental settings violate stated assumptions
No ablation studies on key design choices: which levels need control functionals, kernel sensitivity, failure modes
Theoretical variance bound depends on unknown constants C_l and uncontrolled term ||f_l - f_{l-1}||_{H_l+}
Computational cost of O(m³) control functional construction dismissed without quantification; could be significant in high-dimensional kernel contexts

strengths: Clear problem motivation and positioning relative to existing multilevel methods (Bayesian quadrature, specialized control variates)
Theoretical analysis providing variance bounds with convergence rate improvement when smoothness assumptions hold
Practical applicability to unnormalized densities and broad problem classes without requiring domain expertise
Straightforward methodology combining existing techniques in a natural way
weaknesses: Explicitly incomplete work: authors acknowledge missing optimal sample allocation across levels—a fundamental component for MLMC methods
Severely limited experimental evaluation: only 2 low-dimensional examples (2D, 8D); no high-dimensional experiments despite theory indicating dimension-dependent benefits
Unfair experimental comparisons: MLCF uses QMC/LHS experimental designs while baselines use i.i.d., conflating method improvements with sampling strategy improvements

Weak and incomplete baselines: multilevel Bayesian quadrature dismissed theoretically but never tested empirically; no comparison with Nobile & Tesei (2015) or other multilevel control variate methods
Restrictive theoretical assumptions (bounded domain A1, fill-distance A8, boundary condition A5, smoothness A4, A7) that are violated in experiments, undermining theoretical justification

Unclear novelty over baselines: Proposition 1 is straightforward application of existing control functionals to each MLMC level; contribution of MLCF beyond using CF at finest level not clearly articulated
Dimension-dependent limitations not addressed: fill-distance assumption A8 has exponential dependence on dimension d; no analysis of scalability beyond 8D

Missing critical practical details: kernel selection strategy, optimal number of levels, implementation of constraint A5, detailed computational cost analysis (O(m_l³) terms dismissed without justification)
Incomplete statistical analysis: box plots without confidence intervals, no significance testing, only 50-100 repeats in small experiments
Biased simplified estimator (Remark 1) claimed to have superior MSE but no theoretical proof or justification provided

strengths: Clear problem motivation and positioning relative to existing multilevel and control variate methods, with honest articulation of their limitations
Sound theoretical framework with Theorem 2 proving variance reduction and faster convergence rate O(n^{-(τ_l/d + 1/2)}) compared to MLMC's O(n^{-1/2}) under smoothness assumptions
Practical applicability: works with unnormalized densities, requires no domain expertise, flexible sampling strategies, and straightforward implementation
Consistent empirical improvements over reasonable baselines (MLMC, single-level CF, MCMC) on both ODE and Bayesian inference problems
Well-structured presentation with clear exposition of methodology and background
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is a straightforward combination of control functionals (Oates et al., 2017-2019) and multilevel Monte Carlo (Giles, 2008-2015); Proposition 1 and Theorem 2 are relatively direct applications without substantial new insight

Critical gap between theory and practice: Assumptions A1-A8 are restrictive (bounded domain, high smoothness requirements, RKHS membership), yet authors explicitly acknowledge violating these assumptions in experimental examples (Appendix B), undermining both theoretical validity and empirical validation
Incomplete submission: authors explicitly state the full version will add optimal sample size allocation, which is essential for practical use; paper self-identified as 'initial work'

Limited experimental scope: only 2 examples (2D ODE, 8D Bayesian problem); no systematic evaluation of dimension dependence despite theory claiming advantage when 'dimensionality is not very high'; missing comparison with Multilevel Bayesian Quadrature (mentioned but not compared)

Computational cost inadequately addressed: O(m³) control functional cost per level dismissed as 'not a big issue' without cost-benefit analysis or wall-clock time comparison; unclear when variance reduction justifies additional computation

Missing critical practical guidance: how to verify RKHS membership (A7), how to estimate ||f_l - f_{l-1}||_{H^l_+} (appears in Theorem 2 bound), how to optimally choose m_l, n_l for MLCF; no ablation studies or sensitivity analysis
Simplified estimator (Remark 1) introduced without theoretical analysis of bias-variance tradeoff, only citing superior MSE from prior work
Figure quality and presentation issues: Figures 1-2 are small and difficult to read; limited error bar visualization; notation could be more intuitive

strengths: Novel integration of control functionals with multilevel methods; the motivation is clear and well-illustrated (Figure 1)
Solid theoretical contributions including convergence rate analysis, optimal sample allocation (Theorem 3.3), and extension to variational inference (Theorem 3.4)
Broad applicability: works with unnormalized densities, doesn't require domain expertise, extends to Bayesian inference and variational inference
Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse applications (synthetic, ODE, Bayesian inference, neural networks) with proper error bars and ablations
Practical implementation details provided including hyperparameter selection methods, kernel derivatives, and simplified estimator variants
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: combining existing techniques (CFs + MLMC) is relatively straightforward; the contribution is primarily in execution

Strong theoretical assumptions (A7: RKHS membership, A8: quasi-uniform sampling, smoothness of π and f_l) are difficult to verify a priori and not always satisfied in experiments (e.g., ReLU networks)
Convergence rate advantages O(n^{(-τ/d)-1/2}) vs O(n^{-1/2}) are conditional on large τ and diminish in high dimensions; no systematic study characterizes when MLCF actually beats MLMC in practice

Critical practical gap: optimal sample allocation (Theorem 3.3) requires RKHS norm ∥f_l - f_{l-1}∥_{H_l^+}, but the paper provides no concrete method for computing this in applications; experiments resort to MLMC allocation, undermining novelty
O(m³) computational cost from kernel inversion dismissed without thorough analysis; no wall-clock time comparisons provided for neural network experiments despite O(dn_L³) complexity
Conditions for substantial improvement over baselines are not clearly characterized; experiments show consistent but sometimes modest gains without explaining which problem structures drive benefits
Variational inference extension (Theorem 3.4) is weaker—reduces to single-level CF and shows only marginal empirical improvements; theoretical benefits not convincing
Reproducibility concerns: hyperparameter λ chosen 'heuristically', no code provided, some experimental details unclear (e.g., exact RKHS norm computation for Lotka-Volterra)

strengths: Clear motivation with intuitive figures (Figure 1) illustrating the variance reduction benefit
Solid theoretical contributions: unbiased estimator, variance bounds (Theorem 3.2), and optimal sample allocation (Theorem 3.3)
Broadly applicable: handles unnormalized densities, suitable for Bayesian inference without domain-specific expertise
Extension to variational inference (MLCFRG) with reduced computational complexity
Generally well-written with comprehensive appendices and implementation details
weaknesses: Limited novelty: straightforward combination of existing techniques (control functionals + MLMC) rather than a fundamentally new insight
Restrictive theoretical regime: convergence improvement O(n^{-(τ/d)-1/2}) only when smoothness is high and dimensionality is low; MLMC already achieves O(n^{-1/2})

Strong assumptions (A1-A8) often violated in experiments: Assumption A5 requires boundary conditions on kernels; A8 requires quasi-uniform spacing. Appendix D explicitly states assumptions not fulfilled in experiments, undermining theoretical guarantees
Modest empirical improvements: Figures 2-4 show incremental gains over MLMC/CF; error bars often overlap significantly
Unfair experimental choices: BNN experiments use 1 sample for MLCFRG vs 5 for baselines, conflating variance reduction with sample size selection
Synthetic examples strongly favor the method: functions are kernel linear combinations, not representative of real integrands
Limited baselines: no comparison with other variance reduction techniques (quasi-MC, stratified sampling, other multilevel methods) or MLMC+CF applied independently

Practical implementation complexity not justified: (1) O(m³) kernel cost dismissed without evidence when integrand is cheap, (2) RKHS norm estimation needed for optimal sample allocation adds complexity, (3) fidelity hierarchy construction non-trivial
Loose theoretical bounds from scattered data approximation theory may be uninformative for method comparison
No experiments in high dimensions where theory predicts MLCF underperforms; no ablation studies separating CF vs multilevel benefits
Simplifications (biased estimator in Eq. 11) and hyperparameter selection (via marginal likelihood) add complexity without thorough validation
Statistical significance testing absent; unclear when practitioners should adopt MLCF over simpler alternatives

strengths: Clear motivation combining control functionals with multi-fidelity methods, well-illustrated by Figure 1
Solid theoretical contributions: variance bounds (Theorem 3.2) and optimal sample allocation (Theorem 3.3) with faster convergence rate than MLMC under smoothness assumptions
Broadly applicable to unnormalized densities and MCMC samples, without requiring domain-specific expertise
Useful extension to variational inference (MLCFRG) with computational complexity reduction
Comprehensive experiments across diverse problem types (synthetic, ODEs, Bayesian inference, neural networks)
Well-documented implementation details including kernel derivatives and hyperparameter selection
weaknesses: Convergence rate O(n^(-(τ/d + 1/2))) has dimensional dependence—improvements over MLMC diminish in high dimensions despite authors explicitly stating method works only when 'dimensionality is not very high'
Restrictive assumptions (A1-A8) including quasi-uniform sampling (A8) and boundary conditions on Stein kernels (A5) may not hold in practice

Critical practical barriers inadequately addressed: (1) computing RKHS norms ||f_l - f_{l-1}||_{H_l+} required for optimal allocation is difficult; proposed data-based methods not integrated into framework; (2) O(m³) matrix inversion cost for control functionals not thoroughly addressed; (3) guidance lacking for constructing problem-specific hierarchies

Limited experimental validation of theoretical predictions: neural network examples (d=392-522) don't empirically test dimensional dependence claims, and no comparison with other recent multilevel control variate methods

Technical limitations in Theorem 3.3: constant factor r_l appears loosely bounded, constant m_l/n_l assumption is restrictive, and practical sample allocation requires knowing RKHS norms (vicious circle)
No exploration of failure modes: what happens when smoothness/regularity assumptions are violated? How does method degrade with dimension in practice?
